screens.title: Optimizing Content Delivery for Multi‑tier Architectures
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll build a mental model for how edge services fit into a multi‑tier application. Multi‑tier means separate presentation, application, and data layers; each layer has different delivery needs. Static assets like images and JavaScript benefit from long caching at CloudFront edge locations. Dynamic A P I responses may be partially cached or routed over the AWS backbone to lower latency on cache misses. For private or premium files we use signed URLs or cookies and Origin Access Control so S3 content is never directly public. Edge compute, via CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge, lets you run small, latency‑sensitive logic close to users — for example, lightweight URL rewrites, A/B test routing, or header injection. When traffic isn't HTTP, or you need static IPs and optimized global paths, Global Accelerator provides an entry point onto the AWS network. Route 53 ties it together with latency, geolocation, and failover routing. As you progress through the screens you'll see concrete caching rules, an example Python signed URL flow, when to pick CloudFront versus Global Accelerator, and a hands‑on checklist to configure secure private delivery. Think about a global e‑learning site: which files should be cached for months, which responses must be personalized, and when a signed URL is necessary? Keep that platform in mind as we unpack each service.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next few screens we’re building four measurable competencies. First, you will design content delivery strategies that combine edge services for a complex multi‑tier application. This means choosing where to cache, when to route with Global Accelerator, and how DNS policies in Route 53 should work together. For example, you should be able to map static frontend assets to CloudFront with long TTLs while routing dynamic requests to an ALB behind CloudFront for short cache windows. Second, you will optimize caching for static and dynamic content. That includes selecting cache policies, forwarding the correct headers and query strings, and knowing when to use partial caching to improve repeated request latency. Third and fourth objectives — covered on the next screen — tackle secure delivery and edge compute. Each objective has a competency milestone so you can verify you performed the task correctly. Keep in mind a common pitfall: treating all content the same. As you work through the lesson, think about how you would separate assets, APIs, and premium files in an e‑learning platform.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: This screen expands each objective with a practical verification and a common pitfall. For designing edge strategies, verify by mapping each request type to an origin and edge behavior: static files to an S3 origin with OAC and long TTLs, A P I calls to ALB or A P I Gateway with short cache windows. A common mistake is a one‑size caching rule that either serves stale content or produces low cache hits. For caching strategies, verify by testing cache hit ratios and by forwarding only necessary headers, cookies, or query strings. Misconfiguring forwarded headers often prevents cache consolidation. For secure delivery, verify that direct S3 access is blocked and that signed URLs or cookies grant time‑limited access; a common error is leaving the bucket public or mismanaging key groups. For edge compute and routing, verify function behavior at the edge and test failover with Route 53 policies. The misconception to avoid here is to treat Global Accelerator like a CDN. It optimizes network paths and provides static IPs, but it does not cache content. Keep these verifications in mind as you proceed to the lesson screens.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Verifications
Objective Verifications & Pitfalls
Concrete checks and what to avoid when you implement
Design mapping verification
  • Confirm S3 uses OAC and CloudFront is the only allowed principal for object access.
  • Verify dynamic routes are routed through CloudFront to your ALB or API Gateway origin and observe reduced latency on repeated requests.

Edge & routing verification
  • Deploy small edge functions and validate behavior at CloudFront edge locations.
  • For non‑HTTP traffic, test Global Accelerator routing and failover to secondary regions.
  • Pitfall: expecting Global Accelerator to act as a CDN; it optimizes path but does not cache.

screens.title: Multi‑tier Architecture and the Role of a CDN
screens.narratorSegment: Multi‑tier architecture separates presentation, application, and data. Each tier has distinct delivery needs: static frontend assets are cacheable and benefit from long edge TTLs; application APIs deliver personalized or dynamic data and often need shorter caching or no caching; data stores remain behind the origin. A CDN like CloudFront sits between users and origins and acts as a global cache plus a secure entry point. For static files, CloudFront paired with S3 becomes a high‑throughput, low‑latency distribution: versioned assets can have TTLs of months, yielding high cache hit rates and minimal origin load. For dynamic traffic CloudFront still helps even on cache misses: it connects to your origin over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge location, reducing latency and improving reliability compared to the public internet. A common misconception is that CDNs only serve static content; in reality they also accelerate dynamic traffic, compress responses, and can forward selective headers to support partial caching. Example: a global e‑learning frontend served from S3 via CloudFront with long TTLs for static lessons, while A P I calls for user progress go through CloudFront to an ALB with short cache windows. Takeaway: treat each tier according to mutability, personalization, and cost, and let CloudFront reduce origin load and latency for both static and dynamic needs. What content in your application should never be cached for long?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Multi‑tier & CDN
Definition: Multi‑tier and CDN roles
How the presentation, application, and data layers map to caching and edge behavior.
Presentation (static)
Versioned assets in S3 are ideal for CloudFront with long TTLs to maximize edge caching and reduce origin requests.
Application (dynamic)
APIs behind ALB or API Gateway can be fronted by CloudFront to improve connection performance and optionally partial cache.
Data (origin)
Databases stay behind the origin; caching decisions should never sacrifice data correctness.
Key Takeaway

Map caching policies to tier mutability and personalization: long TTLs for versioned static assets, short/conditional caching for dynamic data.

Example architecture card
E‑learning example
Static course pages and assets in S3 with OAC; CloudFront caches them with long TTLs. API calls for user progress routed to ALB via CloudFront with short caching or no caching where personalization is required.
Common misconception
Believing CDNs only help static files. In practice, a CDN reduces latency for dynamic cache misses and can compress and optimize responses.

screens.title: Origin Access Control (OAC) and Secure Static Delivery
screens.narratorSegment: Origin Access Control prevents direct public access to S3 objects so CloudFront is the only authorized fetcher. This strengthens security by ensuring signed URLs, signed cookies, and CloudFront behaviors control who receives objects. Practically, you create an OAC and apply a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront origin identity to read objects; you also block public access on the bucket configuration. The benefit is twofold: you reduce the attack surface and you force all reads through CloudFront where cache and access policies are enforced. An example use case is premium course videos: the S3 bucket must be private so only signed URLs issued by your application and validated by CloudFront allow playback. A common mistake is leaving the bucket public while also using CloudFront; public buckets bypass your signed URL controls. Verification is simple: request an object directly from the S3 URL and confirm access is denied while the CloudFront signed URL succeeds. Takeaway: OAC is a small configuration change with large security returns — it preserves caching benefits while protecting private content. How would you validate OAC in a staging environment before production?

keyIdea.title: OAC secures S3 origins
keyIdea.text: Use OAC and block public access so CloudFront enforces access control and caching for your S3 objects.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › OAC & Secure Delivery
Origin Access Control (OAC)
Ensure S3 objects are accessible only through CloudFront.
How it works
  • Create an OAC and attach it to your CloudFront distribution's origin.
  • Apply a bucket policy allowing the CloudFront origin identity to GetObject.
  • Block public access at the bucket level so direct S3 URLs are denied.
Quick check
Request S3 URL directly — it should be denied. Use a CloudFront signed URL and confirm the content is delivered.
Example scenario
Premium video in a private S3 bucket. CloudFront distribution uses OAC and signed URLs to serve the video to authenticated users only.
Mistake to avoid
Leaving S3 public in the hope debugging is easier — this bypasses signed URL protections.
Key Takeaway

OAC keeps S3 private while enabling CloudFront to cache and control access to objects.

Verification Card
1) Ensure bucket blocks public access. 2) Attach OAC to CloudFront origin. 3) Test direct S3 URL is denied, then test CloudFront signed URL succeeds.
Why it matters
OAC is required to ensure signed URLs and cookies cannot be circumvented by direct S3 access.

screens.title: Caching Strategy: Static Assets and Cache Policies
screens.narratorSegment: A good static asset caching strategy combines long TTLs with explicit versioning. When files are versioned — for example by embedding a content hash in filenames — you can set very long TTLs, sometimes months or a year, because a new deploy changes the filename and forces update. For CloudFront, create a Cache Policy that instructs how query strings, headers, and cookies build the cache key. For most static assets you should avoid forwarding cookies and unnecessary headers, keeping cache keys compact and maximizing hit ratios. Example: React app assets named app.2a7f. js and styles.34cd. css are ideal for a long TTL. A common mistake is relying on Cache‑Control change without versioning; changing an object in place can lead to stale cached content at edge locations. Another useful configuration is to enable compression at the edge for text assets; CloudFront can compress responses to reduce bandwidth. Verification: deploy a versioned asset, request it repeatedly from different regions, and observe high cache hit rates and minimal origin requests. The core idea: pair long TTLs with immutable naming to get both freshness and high performance. What naming scheme would you use to ensure you never accidentally serve stale files?

keyIdea.title: Immutable assets + long TTLs
keyIdea.text: Versioned filenames with long TTLs maximize cache hit ratios and avoid stale content at the edge.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Caching Strategy
Cache Policy Design
Choose TTLs and what to include in the cache key to balance freshness and hit rate.
Immutable naming
Embed a content hash in filenames so you can use long TTLs safely.
Cache key
Avoid forwarding cookies and unnecessary headers for static assets — keep keys small to increase cache reuse.
Edge compression
Enable Gzip/Brotli at the edge to reduce bandwidth for text assets.
Key Takeaway

Combine versioned filenames with long TTLs and tightly scoped cache keys for optimal static delivery.

Concrete example
GET /static/app.2a7f.js
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, public
CloudFront TTL: 31536000 (1 year)
Origin: S3 (OAC enforced)
Common mistake
Changing files in place without versioned names leads to stale cached content across edge locations.

screens.title: Handling Dynamic Content: Partial Caching and Forwarded Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic A P I responses are less straightforward than static content, but CloudFront still offers advantages. First, even when responses are rarely cacheable, CloudFront reduces latency for cache misses by connecting over the AWS backbone to your origin. Second, you can implement partial caching by creating cache policies that forward only the relevant headers, cookies, or query strings needed to differentiate responses. For instance, if an A P I endpoint returns user‑specific content only when an Authorization header is present, you may choose not to cache those responses. However, for endpoints that return semi‑static data like a leaderboard updated every minute, you can cache for short TTLs and forward query strings that represent the time window or filter. The tradeoffs include complexity of cache key explosion when forwarding too many values versus stale or incorrect personalization when forwarding too few. Compression at the edge can further reduce payload size for dynamic JSON responses. Example: cache product catalog queries for 30 seconds while forwarding category query string but not user cookies. A common misconception is that dynamic means never cache — careful partial caching often yields significant hit ratio improvements. How would you decide which request attributes to forward when building a cache policy?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Dynamic Caching
When to cache dynamic responses
Decide by mutability and personalization level.
Short TTLs for semi‑static data
Cache frequently requested but slowly changing endpoints for seconds to minutes.
Forward minimal attributes
Forward only headers, cookies or query strings required to differentiate correct responses.
Edge compression
Enable Brotli/Gzip for JSON to improve transfer times even on cache misses.
Comparison: Two endpoints
User profile endpoint (highly personalized)
Do not cache; forward Authorization header and user cookie. Ensure correctness over hit ratio.
Public product list (filterable)
Cache for short TTLs and forward only category query string to retain correctness while improving hits.
Mistake
Forwarding too many headers or cookies fragments the cache and lowers hit ratio.

screens.title: Signed URLs: Generating a CloudFront Signed URL (Python)
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough explains the typical Python flow to create CloudFront signed URLs for private objects. The script uses an RSA private key to sign a policy that limits access by expiry time. First, you generate a 2048‑bit RSA pair locally and upload the public key to CloudFront, adding it to a trusted key group. The script reads the local private_key. pem and signs a policy through a CloudFront signer helper that produces a URL containing the signature and expiry. A concrete example from the activity: replace the distribution domain and key id, set the object path and expiration, and run the script to print a signed URL. Security note: keep your private key offline and never embed it in client code. Misconception to avoid: the signed URL itself is not the same as an OAC; OAC keeps the bucket private and the signed URL grants temporary CloudFront access. After you generate a signed URL, test access and confirm that direct S3 requests fail. Takeaway: signed URLs provide short, cryptographically verifiable access to private content without exposing the origin. How would you rotate keys for long‑lived systems?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Signed URL Walkthrough
Python Signed URL Example
A complete local signing flow using an RSA private key and CloudFront signer.
Key steps
  1. Generate RSA key pair locally and keep private key secure.
  2. Upload public key to CloudFront and add to a trusted key group.
  3. Use a Python script to sign a URL with an expiration timestamp.
  4. Test signed URL access and verify direct origin denies requests.
Security reminders
  • Never embed the private key in client apps.
  • Rotate keys and update key groups when needed.
  • Use OAC so signed URLs control CloudFront access while S3 remains private.
Reference script
import datetime
from botocore.signers import CloudFrontSigner
from cryptography.hazmat.backends import default_backend
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import padding

CF_DOMAIN = "d1234abcd.cloudfront.net"
KEY_PAIR_ID = "K123ABCDEF4567"
PRIVATE_KEY_PATH = "private_key.pem"
OBJECT_PATH = "premium-video.mp4"
EXPIRES_AT = datetime.datetime.now() + datetime.timedelta(minutes=5)

def rsa_signer(message):
  with open(PRIVATE_KEY_PATH, 'rb') as key_file:
    private_key = default_backend().load_rsa_private_key(
      key_file.read(),
      password=None
    )
  return private_key.sign(message, padding.PKCS1v15(), hashes.SHA1())

cloudfront_signer = CloudFrontSigner(KEY_PAIR_ID, rsa_signer)

signed_url = cloudfront_signer.generate_presigned_url(
  f"https://{CF_DOMAIN}/{OBJECT_PATH}",
  date_less_than=EXPIRES_AT
)

print(f"Generated Signed URL:
{signed_url}")
print(f"URL expires at: {EXPIRES_AT}")

screens.title: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge
screens.narratorSegment: Edge compute gives you the ability to run logic close to users. CloudFront Functions is designed for very small, high‑performance tasks such as header injection, simple URL rewrites, or A/B testing decisions that must execute in microseconds. Lambda@Edge supports more complex logic and larger runtimes, including calls to external APIs and heavier manipulation, but with higher cold‑start and deployment considerations. Choose CloudFront Functions when you need to manipulate requests and responses in a deterministic, low‑latency way — for example, normalizing URLs for SEO or adding security headers. Use Lambda@Edge when you need more compute or stateful interactions that cannot fit into the constraints of Functions. An example: use a CloudFront Function to strip tracking query parameters before caching, and use Lambda@Edge to perform authentication checks that must call an authentication service. A common misconception is to assume Lambda@Edge is always better because it is more powerful; in practice, the small runtime and cost efficiency of CloudFront Functions make it the appropriate choice for many edge manipulations. Takeaway: match the complexity and latency needs to the edge runtime and prefer the lighter model when possible. What edge task in your app could be moved off the origin and into a CloudFront Function?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Edge Compute
CloudFront Functions
Ultra-fast, small payloads, ideal for rewrites and header tweaks.
Use cases
URL normalization, security header injection, lightweight A/B routing.
Characteristics
Very low latency and cost, but limited runtime and no external network calls in some contexts.
Lambda@Edge
More compute and flexibility for heavier logic at the edge.
Use cases
Complex authentication, personalization that requires external calls, or A/B experiments with server-side variation.
Characteristics
Greater capability but higher cold‑start risk and larger deployment footprints.
Decision guide
If latency is critical and the logic is small, choose Functions. If you need external calls or complex logic, choose Lambda@Edge.

screens.title: AWS Global Accelerator for Non‑HTTP Traffic and Global Paths
screens.narratorSegment: Global Accelerator is a network service that provides static IP addresses and routes traffic onto the AWS global network backbone at the nearest edge location. Use it when you have non‑HTTP/S traffic like gaming, VoIP, or custom TCP/UDP protocols, or when you require predictable entry points (static IPs) and the lowest possible global latency to your regional endpoints. Global Accelerator does not cache content — it optimizes the network path and provides faster failover by directing traffic to the healthiest regional endpoint. CloudFront, on the other hand, is a CDN that caches content globally and supports edge compute for HTTP/S. A typical pattern is to use CloudFront for cached HTTP assets and Global Accelerator in front of ALBs or NLBs for critical dynamic or non‑HTTP services. An example: a real‑time multiplayer game uses Global Accelerator to reduce jitter and provide static IPs to clients, while the game's web storefront and assets are served via CloudFront. A common misconception is to treat Global Accelerator as a CDN; it is not. Takeaway: pick Global Accelerator to optimize path and availability when caching is not the primary need. How would you test failover behavior for your critical A P I endpoints?

Module 11 › Chapter 11.9 › Global Accelerator
When to use Global Accelerator
Optimize network entry and provide static IPs for critical or non‑HTTP traffic.
Use cases
  • Gaming, VoIP, and custom protocols that need low jitter and static IPs.
  • Critical APIs that need the fastest possible traversal of the AWS backbone.
  • Multi‑region active‑active setups that require quick failover.
How it complements CloudFront
CloudFront caches and serves HTTP content; Global Accelerator optimizes the path to regional load balancers and doesn't cache content.
Example
Use Global Accelerator for a game's real‑time matchmaking API and CloudFront for the game's website and static assets.
Mistake
Confusing Global Accelerator with a CDN — it improves routing but does not cache.

screens.title: Route 53 Routing Policies for Global Traffic Management
screens.narratorSegment: Route 53 routing policies let you direct users to the best region based on latency, geography, weight, or health checks. Latency‑based routing sends users to the region with the lowest measured latency for them, improving perceived performance. Geolocation routing can deliver localized content or meet data residency rules by resolving users in a specific country or continent to a chosen region. Weighted routing splits traffic according to ratios, which is useful for incremental rollouts or blue/green testing. Failover routing detects unhealthy primary endpoints and routes traffic to a secondary region automatically, forming a simple disaster‑recovery pattern. A best practice is to combine these with CloudFront and Global Accelerator: use Route 53 to steer initial DNS resolution, CloudFront for caching and edge logic, and Global Accelerator for non‑HTTP traffic. Example: configure latency routing for primary traffic, geolocation overrides for compliance regions, and a health‑checked failover to a standby region for critical APIs. Common misconceptions are assuming DNS changes propagate instantly or that DNS alone solves application failover; DNS-based changes still depend on TTLs and health checks. Takeaway: pick the routing policy that matches your latency, compliance, and release strategy and test failover behaviors under load.

Route 53: Routing policy checklist
Select latency, geolocation, weighted, or failover routing based on your needs.
Latency
Direct users to the region with the lowest latency.
Geolocation
Serve localized content or meet residency requirements.
Weighted
Split traffic for rollouts and experiments.

Latency routing for global users, geolocation override for regulatory regions, weighted routing for canary releases, and health‑checked failover for critical APIs.

screens.title: Layered Security: WAF, Shield, Signed Access
screens.narratorSegment: Layered security means placing controls at multiple points: at the edge, at the distribution, and at the origin. At the edge, AWS WAF protects against common web exploits through rules that block malicious traffic patterns and rate limits. Shield Advanced gives further DDoS protections for high‑value workloads. CloudFront enforces secure access to S3 with OAC, and signed URLs or cookies restrict private content to authenticated users for a limited time. For APIs, you can combine WAF rules with authorization headers and edge functions to reject invalid traffic before it reaches origin services. A typical configuration for a premium content site includes WAF rules for OWASP protections, Shield Advanced for DDoS mitigation, OAC on S3 origins, and signed URLs for premium files. A common mistake is relying on a single control — for example, assuming signed URLs solve DDoS — while they protect only access control. Verification steps include simulating unauthorized direct access to S3, validating WAF blocks for known bad requests, and testing failover and access revocation. Takeaway: apply defense in depth so that edge controls block attacks early and origin protections enforce access policies. Which layer would you tune first when facing repeated bad bots?

Edge protections plus origin controls create a resilient security posture.

Block common web exploits and apply rate limits at CloudFront.
DDoS: Shield
Protect high‑value endpoints with additional DDoS mitigation.
Origin: OAC & Signed URLs

WAF blocks bad requests, CloudFront applies signatures and caching, origin denies direct access through OAC, signed URLs grant temporary playback rights.

screens.title: Hands‑on: Implement Signed URLs for Private Video
screens.narratorSegment: This lab checklist puts the chapter into practice. Start by creating a private S3 bucket and uploading premium-video. mp4, ensuring public access is blocked. Next, create a CloudFront distribution using the S3 bucket as origin and enable Origin Access Control; apply the recommended viewer protocol policy like redirect to HTTPS and set Restrict Viewer Access. While the distribution deploys, generate an RSA key pair locally and upload the public key to CloudFront, then add it to a key group and attach that key group to the distribution's trusted key groups. After deployment, use the Python script we reviewed to sign a URL with an expiry and the private key. Test the signed URL in a browser — you should be able to access the video. Verify direct S3 access is denied and that the URL fails after expiration. Common errors include forgetting to block public access on the S3 bucket or not waiting for distribution deployment before testing. Takeaway: follow each step in order and verify access at each milestone. After finishing the lab, reflect: when would you prefer signed cookies versus signed URLs for your application?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll build a mental model for how edge services fit into a multi‑tier application. Multi‑tier means separate presentation, application, and data layers; each layer has different delivery needs. Static assets like images and JavaScript benefit from long caching at CloudFront edge locations. Dynamic A P I responses may be partially cached or routed over the AWS backbone to lower latency on cache misses. For private or premium files we use signed URLs or cookies and Origin Access Control so S3 content is never directly public. Edge compute, via CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge, lets you run small, latency‑sensitive logic close to users — for example, lightweight URL rewrites, A/B test routing, or header injection. When traffic isn't HTTP, or you need static IPs and optimized global paths, Global Accelerator provides an entry point onto the AWS network. Route 53 ties it together with latency, geolocation, and failover routing. As you progress through the screens you'll see concrete caching rules, an example Python signed URL flow, when to pick CloudFront versus Global Accelerator, and a hands‑on checklist to configure secure private delivery. Think about a global e‑learning site: which files should be cached for months, which responses must be personalized, and when a signed URL is necessary? Keep that platform in mind as we unpack each service.

Over the next few screens we’re building four measurable competencies. First, you will design content delivery strategies that combine edge services for a complex multi‑tier application. This means choosing where to cache, when to route with Global Accelerator, and how DNS policies in Route 53 should work together. For example, you should be able to map static frontend assets to CloudFront with long TTLs while routing dynamic requests to an ALB behind CloudFront for short cache windows. Second, you will optimize caching for static and dynamic content. That includes selecting cache policies, forwarding the correct headers and query strings, and knowing when to use partial caching to improve repeated request latency. Third and fourth objectives — covered on the next screen — tackle secure delivery and edge compute. Each objective has a competency milestone so you can verify you performed the task correctly. Keep in mind a common pitfall: treating all content the same. As you work through the lesson, think about how you would separate assets, APIs, and premium files in an e‑learning platform.

This screen expands each objective with a practical verification and a common pitfall. For designing edge strategies, verify by mapping each request type to an origin and edge behavior: static files to an S3 origin with OAC and long TTLs, A P I calls to ALB or A P I Gateway with short cache windows. A common mistake is a one‑size caching rule that either serves stale content or produces low cache hits. For caching strategies, verify by testing cache hit ratios and by forwarding only necessary headers, cookies, or query strings. Misconfiguring forwarded headers often prevents cache consolidation. For secure delivery, verify that direct S3 access is blocked and that signed URLs or cookies grant time‑limited access; a common error is leaving the bucket public or mismanaging key groups. For edge compute and routing, verify function behavior at the edge and test failover with Route 53 policies. The misconception to avoid here is to treat Global Accelerator like a CDN. It optimizes network paths and provides static IPs, but it does not cache content. Keep these verifications in mind as you proceed to the lesson screens.

Multi‑tier architecture separates presentation, application, and data. Each tier has distinct delivery needs: static frontend assets are cacheable and benefit from long edge TTLs; application APIs deliver personalized or dynamic data and often need shorter caching or no caching; data stores remain behind the origin. A CDN like CloudFront sits between users and origins and acts as a global cache plus a secure entry point. For static files, CloudFront paired with S3 becomes a high‑throughput, low‑latency distribution: versioned assets can have TTLs of months, yielding high cache hit rates and minimal origin load. For dynamic traffic CloudFront still helps even on cache misses: it connects to your origin over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge location, reducing latency and improving reliability compared to the public internet. A common misconception is that CDNs only serve static content; in reality they also accelerate dynamic traffic, compress responses, and can forward selective headers to support partial caching. Example: a global e‑learning frontend served from S3 via CloudFront with long TTLs for static lessons, while A P I calls for user progress go through CloudFront to an ALB with short cache windows. Takeaway: treat each tier according to mutability, personalization, and cost, and let CloudFront reduce origin load and latency for both static and dynamic needs. What content in your application should never be cached for long?

Origin Access Control prevents direct public access to S3 objects so CloudFront is the only authorized fetcher. This strengthens security by ensuring signed URLs, signed cookies, and CloudFront behaviors control who receives objects. Practically, you create an OAC and apply a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront origin identity to read objects; you also block public access on the bucket configuration. The benefit is twofold: you reduce the attack surface and you force all reads through CloudFront where cache and access policies are enforced. An example use case is premium course videos: the S3 bucket must be private so only signed URLs issued by your application and validated by CloudFront allow playback. A common mistake is leaving the bucket public while also using CloudFront; public buckets bypass your signed URL controls. Verification is simple: request an object directly from the S3 URL and confirm access is denied while the CloudFront signed URL succeeds. Takeaway: OAC is a small configuration change with large security returns — it preserves caching benefits while protecting private content. How would you validate OAC in a staging environment before production?

A good static asset caching strategy combines long TTLs with explicit versioning. When files are versioned — for example by embedding a content hash in filenames — you can set very long TTLs, sometimes months or a year, because a new deploy changes the filename and forces update. For CloudFront, create a Cache Policy that instructs how query strings, headers, and cookies build the cache key. For most static assets you should avoid forwarding cookies and unnecessary headers, keeping cache keys compact and maximizing hit ratios. Example: React app assets named app.2a7f. js and styles.34cd. css are ideal for a long TTL. A common mistake is relying on Cache‑Control change without versioning; changing an object in place can lead to stale cached content at edge locations. Another useful configuration is to enable compression at the edge for text assets; CloudFront can compress responses to reduce bandwidth. Verification: deploy a versioned asset, request it repeatedly from different regions, and observe high cache hit rates and minimal origin requests. The core idea: pair long TTLs with immutable naming to get both freshness and high performance. What naming scheme would you use to ensure you never accidentally serve stale files?

Dynamic A P I responses are less straightforward than static content, but CloudFront still offers advantages. First, even when responses are rarely cacheable, CloudFront reduces latency for cache misses by connecting over the AWS backbone to your origin. Second, you can implement partial caching by creating cache policies that forward only the relevant headers, cookies, or query strings needed to differentiate responses. For instance, if an A P I endpoint returns user‑specific content only when an Authorization header is present, you may choose not to cache those responses. However, for endpoints that return semi‑static data like a leaderboard updated every minute, you can cache for short TTLs and forward query strings that represent the time window or filter. The tradeoffs include complexity of cache key explosion when forwarding too many values versus stale or incorrect personalization when forwarding too few. Compression at the edge can further reduce payload size for dynamic JSON responses. Example: cache product catalog queries for 30 seconds while forwarding category query string but not user cookies. A common misconception is that dynamic means never cache — careful partial caching often yields significant hit ratio improvements. How would you decide which request attributes to forward when building a cache policy?

This walkthrough explains the typical Python flow to create CloudFront signed URLs for private objects. The script uses an RSA private key to sign a policy that limits access by expiry time. First, you generate a 2048‑bit RSA pair locally and upload the public key to CloudFront, adding it to a trusted key group. The script reads the local private_key. pem and signs a policy through a CloudFront signer helper that produces a URL containing the signature and expiry. A concrete example from the activity: replace the distribution domain and key id, set the object path and expiration, and run the script to print a signed URL. Security note: keep your private key offline and never embed it in client code. Misconception to avoid: the signed URL itself is not the same as an OAC; OAC keeps the bucket private and the signed URL grants temporary CloudFront access. After you generate a signed URL, test access and confirm that direct S3 requests fail. Takeaway: signed URLs provide short, cryptographically verifiable access to private content without exposing the origin. How would you rotate keys for long‑lived systems?

CloudFront Functions is designed for very small, high‑performance tasks such as header injection, simple URL rewrites, or A/B testing decisions that must execute in microseconds. An example: use a CloudFront Function to strip tracking query parameters before caching, and use Lambda@Edge to perform authentication checks that must call an authentication service. Challenge yourself: for each asset type in your application, name the correct CDN policy and access control you would apply. Key Concepts — Part 1 means tailor delivery by content type: cache immutables long-term, secure private objects with oac and signed access, and use edge compute where latency matters.. In practical terms, three core ideas to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A few final points to carry into implementation. Origin Access Control is essential when using S3 as a CloudFront origin so that signed URLs and cookies cannot be bypassed. Edge compute choices matter: CloudFront Functions for tiny, fast changes; Lambda@Edge for heavier logic. Global Accelerator provides improved network paths and static IPs for non‑HTTP or critical traffic but does not cache; it complements CloudFront and Route 53. Finally, layered security — WAF at the edge, Shield for DDoS, OAC for origins, and signed access for private content — prevents single points of failure. Keep a habit of verification: test direct origin denial, test signed URL expiry behavior, measure cache hit ratios, and simulate failover.
